To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
fat addition to a fibrous diet improves feed:gain without affecting ADG and that increasing the slaughter weight improves the desirable carcass traits.
dietary fat inclusion improves feed efficiency, carcasses of rabbits slaughtered at heavier weights are more desirable for marketing, and there is no advantage in using vegetable fat over animal fat.
the addition of fat to the diet of growing rabbits increases their feed:gain ratio and the weight of carcass and body fat, but does not affect ADG.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of dietary fat on growth, feed intake, feed:gain ratio, carcass characteristics and body composition of growing rabbits.
the effects of fat addition to fibroous diets on the growth performance, carcass characteristics and body chemical composition of rabbits killed at 2.0,2.25, or 2.5kg.
the influence of dietary fat and slaughter weight on the growth performance, carcass traits, and body chemical compositions of rabbits.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the addition of fat to the diets of rabbits fed high-fiber diets improves feed:gain and increases the weight and the quality of the carcass.
the inclusion of fat in the diet increases the fat content in the carcass, but the effect of fat inclusion on carcass composition is not significant.
the use of 3% fat in the diets of rabbits increased the body fat content and the weights of perirenaI and scapular depots, without impairing the carcass characteristics or the feed:gain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
fat addition to diets containing high levels of fiber improves the feed:gain without affecting carcass quality, but increasing slaughter weight improves the carcass quality and the feed:gain.
increasing dietary fat improves carcass characteristics, but the effect of fat addition on carcass characteristics is less than that of slaughter weight.
the inclusion of 3% fat in the diet of the rabbit increases the body fat content and the weights of the fat depots.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of fat in the diet of rabbits increases carcass fat content and improves feed:gain ratios.
rabbits can tolerate high levels of dietary fat without adverse effects.
rabbits fed diets with added fat had higher body fat contents and heavier carcasses, and that rabbits slaughtered at higher weights had heavier carcasses with more desirable retail cuts.
